title: Quantum polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
formal: Do there exist a constant \(C>0\) and a uniform quantum algorithm A with polynomial running time such that, for every rational matrix \(B\in Q^{d\times n}\) with \(d\ge n\ge 1\) and linearly independent columns, A outputs a nonzero \(z\in Z^{n}\) satisfying \(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}\le n^{C} \lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L}(B))\) with probability at least \(2/3\)?
definitions: The full matrix, dimensions and every rational entry are given classically; rationals use signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Let N be the total encoding length. \(\mathrm{L}(B)=\{Bz:z\in Z^{n}\}, \lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{\Vert v\Vert _{2}:0\ne v\in \mathrm{L}\}\), and \(\Vert v\Vert _{2}=(\sum_{i} v_{i}^{2})^{1/2}\). Approximation depends on rank n rather than the ambient dimension d or N. Use a uniform quantum circuit computation with classical polynomial-time control, polynomially many qubits initially in computational basis states, gates \(H=2^{- 1/2}[[1,1],[1,- 1]], T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\) and CNOT, and computational-basis measurements with classical feed-forward. The classical input bits may be copied into input qubits. One polynomial \(p(N)\) bounds total classical bit operations, gate applications, measurements and output bits on every branch. Classical control and circuit generation are uniform in the input length and use no advice or oracle; a unit-cost quantum random-access oracle for the input is not supplied. The output is a binary-encoded integer coefficient vector, required to be nonzero on every branch; the norm guarantee may fail with probability at most \(1/3\). The constants C and p are independent of all inputs. There is no uniqueness, average-case, ideal-lattice, modular or conditioning promise.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
why: Isolate the potential power of quantum computation in the central polynomial-factor regime of worst-case lattice approximation.

importance.reason: A foundational quantum-algorithm question with broad relevance to lattice complexity and computational cryptography. The model and accuracy combination is distinct from both existing classical approximation and quantum exact-search cards.

progress.text: Regev establishes a quantum worst-case-to-average-case reduction involving GapSVP, SIVP and LWE at specified parameters.
Bennett’s survey documents the large unresolved polynomial-factor region in general SVP complexity.
The posted Regev version preserves the earlier theorem, with a proof correction, rather than announcing a new lattice algorithm.

context_blocks.text: A short lattice vector may be hidden by cancellation among much longer basis columns. The task is to find an integer combination with length bounded relative to the shortest possible nonzero combination. Allowing a factor \(n^{C}\) is a substantial relaxation of exact shortest-vector search, yet remains far stronger than the guarantees of basic polynomial-time lattice reduction.

The existing TCS-6667 asks the same approximate search question for a classical randomized algorithm. TCS-7169 instead asks about a quantum algorithm for exact SVP. This card distinguishes the missing intermediate combination: quantum computation with a polynomial approximation factor. A classical solution of the matching approximation target would qualify here, but a quantum solution would not automatically give a classical one.

Regev’s worst-case to average-case reduction connects specified GapSVP and SIVP tasks to Learning With Errors. Its consequence has a direction: a suitable efficient LWE solver yields quantum algorithms for the lattice tasks in the theorem. It does not establish an unrestricted equivalence between arbitrary polynomial-factor search SVP and every LWE parameter family.

The distinction matters for interpretation of a breakthrough. An algorithm satisfying this card would substantially change our understanding of quantum lattice reduction. Its effect on a particular cryptographic assumption would still depend on the approximation exponent, the exact lattice problem and the reduction parameters. Merely naming LWE is insufficient to infer that every parameter choice has been broken.

Rank and bit length are separate variables. Increasing coefficients must not be mistaken for increasing the allowed approximation factor, and a polynomial algorithm must include the cost of reading and manipulating their binary representations. The specified gate model permits ordinary quantum computation while excluding an additional oracle resource hidden in a data-access convention.
